summary:
Humanities is a 2D pixel-art survival game set on Mars in the year 2045. You play the lead systems planner for a fictional mission. Before launch, you decide what to bring on a limited budget and cargo weight. Then you live with those choices on Mars.

Each day starts with a briefing from mission control. You pick your actions, watch what happens, and read an evening report. Power, life support and radiation protection all depend on each other, so a decision today can cause trouble a few days later. When a solar storm hits, you see how your earlier choices helped or hurt the crew.

Before key events the game asks you to predict what will happen. Short science cards then explain the real engineering behind it, with sources. At the end, a debrief shows how your decisions linked together and lets you ask "what if?"

A full mission takes about 5 to 8 minutes, so it is easy to replay and try a different strategy. The game is built for young learners and uses NASA open data where it can. It is a fictional mission and is not endorsed by NASA.
details:
Humanities is a browser-based 2D pixel-art game about running a Mars outpost. The player is the lead systems planner for a fictional 2045 mission. You spend a limited budget on equipment, and cargo weight is limited too. Then you manage the colony day by day: a morning briefing, an action choice, a simulation step, and an evening report. Power, life support and radiation protection are connected, so one decision can affect the others days later. A seeded solar storm event tests those choices. The same seed gives the same result, so a run can be replayed and compared.

Benefits

Players learn real engineering trade-offs by living with them instead of reading about them. Before key events the game asks for a prediction, then shows what happened and why, with science cards that cite their sources. The debrief shows how decisions linked together and lets players ask "what if?" Each mission takes 5 to 8 minutes, so it is easy to replay.

Intended impact

We want young learners to see that space exploration is about trade-offs, not just rockets. The game is meant to spark curiosity. We do not claim it is proven to improve learning, and it is not a prediction of real survival.

Tools and technology

  • JavaScript and the Phaser game engine
  • HTML and CSS for the interface
  • Automated tests for the resource engine
  • Git and GitHub for version control
  • Vercel for deployment
  • No backend, database or AI APIs, so it runs entirely in the browser on any normal computer

Creativity

The game does more than show a dashboard. It has a story, a pixel-art outpost, a launch cinematic and dialogue between mission control and the crew. The "chain reaction" design makes consequences delayed and connected. The title also carries themes: Home, Unity, Meaning, Adaptation and New beginnings.

What we considered

  • The audience, ages 7 to 12, so text is readable and the game works on mobile and with accessibility needs
  • Scientific honesty: real and simulated values are labelled, and the game is clearly fictional and not NASA-endorsed
  • Reliable engineering: a deterministic engine that can be tested
  • Scope: we built the game in small milestones so it would be finished and working by the deadline
